turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Sunday, the twenty-seventh of September. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go.
Three things this morning. A seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, rejected in four words.
Singapore crossed a demographic line on Thursday and nobody rang a bell. [curious] It's in a footnote.
And the most photographed railway in Asia has not run to Kandy since November.
[amused] That last one is going to annoy a lot of holiday plans.
Start with Hormuz. On Thursday Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, told reporters in New York that Tehran had passed Washington a seven-day plan through Qatar.
Seven days to what?
To reopening the strait. And he published the running order, which diplomats almost never do. American steps on days one to five. The strait opens on day six. Nuclear talks resume on day seven.
[thoughtful] So it's a calendar, not a position.
That's what made it different.
What did Iran want for it?
The naval blockade of its ports lifted. Sanctions on its oil sales waived. About twelve billion US dollars in frozen assets released. And a regional ceasefire covering Lebanon and Yemen too.
And in exchange, the chokepoint.
The chokepoint and the table.
Okay. And the answer?

[deadpan] Saturday, outside the White House. Quote: I reject their proposal. There was more. He said, they want to make a deal and I think that's fine. I'd like to make a deal, too. But that deal would not be acceptable. And in the same scrum he described the waterway in the first person plural. We have total control of the Hormuz Strait.
[pause] That's a striking way to describe a strait you don't own.

It is. And the Chinese state wire chose exactly that sentence when it ran the story. Without any editorial line at all. It just put the conditional Iranian proposal next to the claim of ownership and let the reader do the work. It is. The same day it gave separate prominent play to Araghchi calling West Asian security — quote — integrated and indivisible. Meeting the Saudi foreign minister, the Arab League, agreeing shipping lanes with Oman.
So force on one side of the ledger, consensus on the other. What does Doha's coverage do differently?
Al Jazeera prints the plan's terms in full, and sets it against fuel prices running into an American electoral cycle.
Meaning Washington is the one holding a clock.

Meaning that. And here's the number underneath it. American retail diesel hit six dollars fifty a gallon on Thursday, against five dollars sixty-one in August. A hundred and seven point nine million barrels. The thinnest in four decades.
[exhales] Okay, so there is a clock.
Seventh month of the war, and the strait that carried a fifth of the world's traded oil and gas is still shut.
What do the analysts think the plan is actually worth?

Thomas Warrick at the Atlantic Council won't even call it an event. He says the best we can hope for is that it leads to further discussions, to clarify what preconditions Washington is willing to work with.
So the ceiling is clarification.

Not agreement. And Paul Musgrave at Georgetown's Qatar campus adds the mechanism — a president who doesn't want to end a war on unfavourable terms may, after a bad November, reach for unilateral action rather than look beaten.
[skeptical] Which would make Saturday's four words a schedule.
Rather than a position. Yes.
Right. Home. What happened on Thursday?
Population in Brief went up. Twenty-one point four per cent of Singapore citizens are now sixty-five or older.
And the line is?
Twenty-one. The United Nations definition of a super-aged society. It's in footnote nine of the same document. The phrase does not appear in the headline text.
[thoughtful] That's a civilisational marker filed as an annotation.

It was thirteen point seven per cent in twenty-sixteen. Here's the one that lands. The old-age support ratio — working-age citizens per citizen over sixty-five — is two point eight. It was four point seven a decade ago. The report's own projection is two point two by twenty thirty-five. Twenty-six thousand and seventy-one citizen births last year. Down ten point eight per cent in one year. Fertility zero point eight seven — a record low.
And yet the population went up.

Six point two million. Up one point six per cent. And the report is unusually direct about why — mainly more work permit holders in construction, for Changi Terminal Five and the Marina Bay Sands expansion.
So the growth is a building site.
The economist Walter Theseira makes exactly that point. Demand for foreign workers is concentrated in construction and domestic work, and an ageing population generates the care demand itself.
[wry] The country didn't get more populous. It got older and built a terminal.

And the harder point needs no economist. Births fell ten point eight per cent, marriages fell five point six, and the citizen count still rose zero point seven. Twenty-five thousand and ninety-four new citizenships.
So the growth line is an intake line.

The document says immigration keeps the citizen population from shrinking. That's the polite version of the same sentence. Three central banks raised rates inside nine days, and the dollar declined to notice. On the sixteenth. Twenty-five basis points, to three point seven five to four per cent. Unanimous, twelve to nil. First increase since twenty twenty-three. The statement says plainly, inflation remains elevated. The European Central Bank had gone six days earlier. The Bank of Japan followed on the eighteenth, to one point two five per cent.
Which is what, historically?
Highest since April nineteen ninety-five. And its shortest gap between hikes since nineteen ninety.
[exhales] That's a synchronised re-tightening.

The ten-year went to five point zero six per cent, up seventeen basis points on the week. The real ten-year up twenty-one, to two point eight three. Two-year to ten-year is plus fifty-six basis points. But it steepened because the long end sold off, not because the front end rallied. Term premium. Nothing in it is an easing trade. And there's an oddity — the twenty-year sits above the thirty-year. Five point five four against five point four nine.
Inverted at the very long end. That's usually supply indigestion.
That's where it shows up first.
Okay, the portfolio read.

This is the part that matters. A global aggregate bond fund is down two point six four per cent for the year, and down one point six four over twelve months. A world equity fund up about nineteen over the same twelve.
[pause] So the bond sleeve returned less than nothing.
Through a period when equities returned nineteen. It isn't hedging. It's being paid for.
And that's the uncomfortable bit, isn't it, because —

Because an inflation shock is exactly the shock that eventually takes both legs down together. Yes. Holds the contradiction. Real yields at two point eight three should punish it, and on the month they do — down six point seven per cent. Over twelve months it's still up about thirteen point seven.
War bid versus real yields.
And the real yield is currently winning. Eighty-four thousand one hundred and eleven dollars. About thirty-three per cent below its high, falling while equities sit near theirs.
Because three hiking central banks is the worst possible input for it.
It's trading as the inverse of the global cost of money.
So what's the anomaly this week?
[curious] The dollar didn't rally.
Wait — really? With a hawkish Fed and a five per cent ten-year?
The dollar index fell zero point two six per cent. Part of it is mechanical, the Bank of Japan hiked too. But it's a broad basket.
So what's it pricing?

Something the rates market isn't. A consumer that's already broken. And the same week, Michigan consumer sentiment printed forty-eight point one. Down from fifty-one point seven. Alongside a one point six per cent beat in core capital goods orders.
[thoughtful] So the household says recession and the capex says expansion.
One of them is wrong.
And a correction, I'm told.

We printed Friday's ten-year as five point one zero in yesterday's issue. Treasury's own par curve says five point zero six. We take Treasury's. A rule took effect two days before anyone could read it. Commerce published a temporary final rule on Thursday restricting polysilicon imports by anyone judged to be stockpiling. Its own dates paragraph says it is effective the twenty-second of September.
And it was published?
The twenty-fourth. No comment period.
What does it actually do?

Caps a new importer of record at twelve kilogrammes of high-purity silicon a week. Fifty-five photovoltaic cells in modules. It's policing the run-up to the fourth of December, when minimum import prices bite. Twenty-one dollars a kilo for polysilicon.
Against what world price?
About five dollars twenty-seven in January, per the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
That's a four-times floor.
And here's the trap they identify. Makers of semiconductor-grade polysilicon depend on the much larger solar-grade market for economies of scale.
So suppressing solar demand could hurt the thing the rule exists to protect.
Which is two point four per cent of global polysilicon production.
[pause] The rule doesn't distinguish?

No line between semiconductor-grade and solar-grade. Every listed code, same restriction. And it names no country. Tim Pawlenty at the Solar Energy Industries Association. He says imposing tariffs and price floors on solar materials will create new challenges for American manufacturers and raise energy costs for families and businesses.
Okay. Home lab — give me the one that matters.

A tiling rewrite of the processor matrix multiply merged into llama dot cpp on Saturday. Prefill goes from sixteen point three tokens a second to sixty-seven point one. On a twenty-seven-billion-parameter model at a two-thousand-token prompt. On V N N I.
And on what most people actually own?
[deadpan] One point seven.
[sighs] There it is.
Fifteen to twenty-five point four on A V X two. Which is every Zen two and Zen three part, every pre-Ice-Lake Intel, and the whole second-hand Xeon crowd.
And it's prefill, not generation.
Prompt processing. Does nothing for token generation, which is the thing people complain about.
Any accuracy cost?
Small but real. Max single-scalar error around five times ten to the minus four. And nobody in the thread published a perplexity or divergence check.
On a path that now runs by default.
That's the gap.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every single morning with this one.
[laughs] What have we got?

Beekeeping. And the whole craft rests on a gap of nine and a half millimetres. Bees maintain a working passage of about seven millimetres, give or take two. Give them less than six and they cement it closed with propolis. Give them more than nine and a half and they build comb across it.
And in between?
They leave it alone. Which means the frame lifts out. Clean. As many times as you like.
[gasps] So before that you had to destroy the colony to get the honey.

Langstroth's patent, the fifth of October eighteen fifty-two. Everything downstream depends on it — inspection, disease control, queen management, the extractor, migratory pollination. One measurement.
Okay, the numbers. How big is this?
America ran two point six million producing colonies last year, for a hundred and thirty-four million pounds of honey. A crop worth three hundred and sixty-one and a half million dollars.
And the losses?
Fifty-five point six per cent in twenty twenty-four to twenty-five. The worst since the survey began in twenty ten.
[pause] More than half.
Meanwhile Berlin's beekeeper numbers more than tripled between two thousand and five and twenty twenty-two. Same in Zurich, Paris, Toronto.
So the hobby is growing while the animal husbandry gets harder.
That's the honest trend line.
What hooks people?

The Flow Hive. February twenty fifteen, two Australians put a hive with a tap on a crowdfunding site asking for seventy thousand Australian dollars. Over twelve million. Nearly twenty-five thousand orders from more than a hundred and thirty countries.
[laughs] Honey on tap.

Honey without opening the box. And the criticism is documented — it was marketed as harvesting without disturbing the bees, and experienced beekeepers said that misrepresented the importance of hive maintenance.
Did the company respond?

Its inventor reframed it to say it only changes the harvesting process. And on the company's own forum a user logged the practical failure — lots of issues with leaking honey out through the brood box and onto the ground.
What does it cost?
Eight hundred and ninety-nine US dollars in cedar. And a spare set of frames runs two hundred and fifty-nine to four hundred and forty-nine.
And a normal extractor?
Three hundred and nine ninety-five.
[scoffs] So the spare frames cost more than the machine they replace.
That's the line.
What's the fight inside the hobby?

Whether to treat for varroa at all. Michael Bush is the treatment-free voice — foundationless comb, no treatments, queens bred from survivors. His blunt claim is that whether you treat or not, they all die anyway quite often.
And the other side?
Randy Oliver, a biologist running a commercial operation. He says too often the underlying cause is a lack of effective management that lets a mite infestation overwhelm a colony.
Is there anything genuinely new?

Extended-release oxalic acid strips. Trial efficacy around ninety-five to ninety-seven per cent. But the breakthrough is the label, not the kill rate — no temperature restriction, and approved with honey supers in place.
So you can treat during the flow.
Which no beekeeper has previously been able to do.
And the robot? I've heard about the robot.
Beewise. Computer vision, a heat chamber, fifty million dollars in a Series D, twelve hundred and forty units deployed.
[curious] Does it work?

Its website claims seventy per cent lower colony loss. Its chief executive's public figures imply about eighty. He's separately said eighty. One company, one year. And the reporting notes there are no peer-reviewed studies, no third-party audits and no independent verification.
What would settle it?
One independent season-long comparison. Nobody has published one.
And here? Could I keep bees in Singapore?

[wry] That's the finding. Nobody will tell you clearly. The national wildlife authority's public page on bees contains no beekeeping regulation at all. It's a safety page. Back away, call the helpline.
And the operators?
The most established one declines to answer. He says it falls in grey, and that it would be a case-by-case decision by the authority.
[laughs] That is a very Singaporean non-answer.
And on a condominium balcony there is no official answer at all. The binding constraint is the management corporation's by-laws and one neighbour's complaint.
So what's the realistic route?
Stingless bees. Singapore has a hundred and thirty-three bee species on its first national checklist. Seven of them have no sting whatsoever.
And the European bee doesn't work here?
Everything in the manuals assumes a winter. No winter means no brood break, which means no pause in the mite's breeding cycle.
And the local bee?
Apis cerana. Colonies of six or seven thousand workers against the European bee's fifty thousand. And it absconds far more readily.
So the failure mode isn't winter loss.
It's the whole colony leaving.
[thoughtful] That's a completely different craft.
Does the money ever work? One hive, year one, is three hundred and fifty to eight hundred dollars. The American average colony yields fifty-one point seven pounds at two dollars sixty-nine wholesale.
Which is about a hundred and forty dollars of honey.
And year one produces essentially no surplus at all, because the colony spends its first season drawing comb.
So when do you break even?
On the boxes, roughly year three. On the extractor, [pause] never. Quick round. Culture — the longest number-one run in the history of the Hot One Hundred is sitting at number two in Britain.
[curious] How does that work?

Ella Langley's twenty-third week at the top of the American chart is the same week she's behind Sienna Spiro on the British one. Both true. Naming the chart is the whole job — and we didn't name it yesterday, so that's a second correction. The third-generation Ray-Ban Meta went on sale Wednesday. Four hundred and forty-nine US dollars, and Singapore is a launch market — six hundred and sixty-nine Singapore dollars. Two of the three headline features aren't in the box. The spatial audio capture ships later this year, and landscape capture wasn't available to reviewers.
And the battery?
Nine hours claimed. No independent measurement exists. The nearest number anywhere is a reviewer getting about five hours on the previous model.
Which the new one supposedly beats by an hour. [laughs] Right.
The Atelier did fountain pens. And the line of the week comes from a seller on the Fountain Pen Network who handled a hundred and sixty-two new Viscontis.
How many wrote properly? [gasps] Out of a hundred and sixty-two?
Over eighteen months. And here's the one that will surprise you — for a Pilot Custom Eight Two Three, Singapore is about thirty-one per cent under the American list price.
[amused] That never happens.

Travel. Two things. Book by Tuesday if you're buying a long-haul ticket — the sustainable fuel levy applies to tickets issued from the first of October. A business fare to London goes from sixty-five dollars twenty of tax to ninety dollars eighty. Thirty-nine per cent.
And the second?

The Grand Tour is Sri Lanka's hill country. And the train everyone photographs has not run to Kandy since November. Cyclone Ditwah. Six sections of track obliterated near Balana. Sixty-nine billion rupees of damage at two hundred and twenty-three locations. Colombo services terminate at Rambukkana. An hour out. Full restoration is targeted for the thirty-first of December.
So you can't do it.
Only the eastern half — Nanu Oya to Ella to Badulla, reached by road. And here's the accident: that's the better half.
[laughs] Of course it is.

The trip reports have said so for years. And one more thing — February and March are the hill country's real window, not December. Nuwara Eliya gets a hundred and eighty-three millimetres over fifteen wet days in December. In February, seventy-three millimetres over seven.
[thoughtful] So the guidebooks are sending people in the wrong month.
And to the wrong side of the watershed. Ella is on the Uva flank, so it's wettest exactly when the guides send you.
Okay. Close us out.

The Undercurrent is Bangladesh, and the word is jhut. It's the trade term for what falls off a cutting table. Between four hundred thousand and five hundred and seventy-seven thousand tonnes a year. And almost none of it is buried.
Where does it go?

Swept into sacks, sold at the gate, and hand-sorted by about two hundred thousand people. Seven in ten of them women. T-shirts in Pabna. Sweaters in Gaibandha. Blankets in Bogura. Rope, mattress stuffing, kiln fuel. The share that can't be sold at all is five to ten per cent.
So this is a circular economy.

It has been for forty years. Nobody called it that. In July, European rules made it illegal for large companies to destroy unsold clothing, and a traceability regime is coming. Overnight jhut stopped being rubbish and became a compliance asset.
[pause] Here's my question. Who was getting paid?
A factory owner under a politically connected collector receives two to four taka a kilo. The market rate is forty.
And he can't refuse.
He can't refuse. And the women sorting it earn two hundred to two hundred and sixty taka a day. Ninety-four per cent have only a verbal agreement. None has social security.
So when the formal channel arrives —
It selects the five to seven per cent that's clean, cotton and documentable, and routes it to industrial recyclers with brand-approved paperwork.
And leaves the rest.
Leaves the blends, the small pieces, the material only a person can sort. And the informal economics depended on cross-subsidy from exactly the fraction being removed.
[thoughtful] So the circular economy isn't arriving. It's being taken.

That's the argument. And the researcher who studied it, Lone Riisgaard, makes the sharpest point — the environmental benefits of the new channel should be proven to outweigh the existing ones before jhut is appropriated away from the clusters.
Has anyone run that proof? [exhales] And there's a number that sits underneath all of it, isn't there.
Europe destroys between two hundred and sixty-four thousand and five hundred and ninety-four thousand tonnes of unsold textiles a year.
And Bangladesh sweeps up four hundred to five hundred and seventy-seven thousand.

The two numbers are the same size. A rule written in the language of documentation will always favour whoever is already documented. The informal sector isn't, by definition. It's not being outcompeted. It's being defined out.
[thoughtful] And three women on a tarpaulin with hand shears triple the value of what's in front of them, and no passport records it.
By the new definition, that isn't circular at all.
[sighs] That's a good one.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-eight pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
